```{r}
library(dplyr)


df <- data.frame(
x = c(5, 1, 4, NA, NA, NA, 2, 1),
y = c(5, NA, 3, 2, 5, NA, 2, 1),
z = c(1, 4, 2, 5, 2, NA, 5, 4),
t = c(4, 2, NA, 1, 5, 2, 3, 3)
)

# Use collaborative filtering to predict User 2's preference for Movie 6. The data frame is shown below:

cor(df$y, df$x, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor(df$y, df$z, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor(df$y, df$t, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

mean(df$y,na.rm= TRUE)  
mean(df$t,na.rm = TRUE)
mean(df$x,na.rm = TRUE)

# User 2 preference for movie 6 based on only user 4's preference for movie 6, 
# due to NA value present in formula for user 1 preference for movie 6
User_Y_MPref_6 = ((.72)/(.96+.72))*(2-2.857143)+3
User_Y_MPref_6

```
```{r}
# Use Pearson correlation to determine which movie is the most similar to Movie 1.

dfTransposed= t(df)

cor(dfTransposed, method = "pearson", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

#Thus, movie 5 is most similar to movie 1 based on pearson correlation with an r value of about .97
```
```{r}
#Apply mean imputation grouped according to region to fill in missing values in the column for "Agriculture" and the column for "Industry" for the countries dataset
dfc <- read.csv("http://manctsui.github.io/datasets/countries.csv")


dfImp <- dfc |>
  select(Region, Agriculture, Industry) |>
  group_by(Region) |>
  mutate(Agriculture = ifelse(is.na(Agriculture), mean(Agriculture,na.rm = TRUE),    Agriculture)) |>
  mutate(Industry =ifelse(is.na(Industry), mean(Industry, na.rm = TRUE), Industry)) |>
  ungroup()

dfImp

#How many NA's did you have to fill from each region?

dfc |>
  select(Region, Industry, Agriculture) |>
  group_by(Region) |>
  count(is.na(Industry) & is.na(Agriculture))

# From Latin Amer/Carib there were 2 NA's 
# From Northern Africa there was 1 NA
# From Northern America there were 2 NA's
# From Oceania there were 5 NA's
# From Sub-Saharan Africa there were 2 NA's
# From Western Europe there were 3 NA's

```
```{r}
library(plotly)
df3 <- data.frame(
temp = c(79, 74, 73, 76, 82, 72, 71, 79, 83, 70, 73, 75, 77),
chirps = c(44, 40, 38, 43, 48, 37, 34, 45, 51, 32, 35, 42, 43)
)

lm(temp ~ chirps, data = df3)

df3 |>
plot_ly(x= ~temp, y= ~chirps)


r = cor(df3$temp, df3$chirps)
tempmean = mean(df3$temp)
sdtemp = sd(df3$temp)
chirpsmean = mean(df3$chirps)
sdchirps = sd(df3$chirps)

#you can compute the linear regression using the above statistics-
# find slope:
m = r*(sdtemp/sdchirps)
m

#find intercept:
b = tempmean - (m*chirpsmean)
b

# This gives us the equation above since the slope m = .714 and 
# the intercept b = 46.474
```

## Quarto

Quarto enables you to weave together content and executable code into a finished document. To learn more about Quarto see <https://quarto.org>.

## Running Code

When you click the **Render** button a document will be generated that includes both content and the output of embedded code. You can embed code like this:

```{r}
1 + 1
```

You can add options to executable code like this

```{r}
#| echo: false
2 * 2
```

The `echo: false` option disables the printing of code (only output is displayed).
